Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Tuesday, 15 October 2024 at 2pm
(Day 055)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu SC for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, good afternoon.
MR MUSTON: The first witness this afternoon is Dr Tom
Morrison. He is sitting there lonely at the panel table.
<THOMAS GALE MORRISON, affirmed: [2pm]
<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON:
MR MUSTON: Q. Dr Morrison, could you state your full
name for the record, please?
A. Yes, my name's Thomas Gale Morrison.
Q. You are currently working as an unaccredited registrar
in neurosurgery at St Vincent's Hospital?
A. Yes.
Q. That's a role that you have held since February 2023?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. I think next year, in 2025, you will be commencing the
surgical education and training program in neurosurgery?
A. Yes.
Q. At St Vincent's?
A. At Liverpool, actually.
Q. At which hospital?
A. Liverpool.
Q. Prior to that, you've held roles at Royal Prince
Alfred Hospital as an unaccredited registrar in
neurosurgery?
A. Yes.
Q. I think from February 2020 to February 2023?
A. Yes, that's correct, three years.
Q. And before that you were a resident at RPA
from February 2019 to February 2020?
A. Yes.
Q. And before that an intern at RPA?
A. That's correct.
Q. You are also the junior vice president of the
Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation?

A. Yes.
Q. Broadly known as ASMOF, and a member of the AMA
council?
A. Yes.
Q. And an executive member of the AMA Doctors-in-Training
Committee since 2020?
A. That's correct.
Q. You have prepared a statement to assist the Inquiry
with its work?
A. I have.
Q. That statement is dated 4 October 2024?
A. Yes.
Q. Have you had a chance to read that statement before
giving your evidence today?
A. Yes, I have.
Q. That is to say, just before, as opposed to when you
wrote it?
A. I have, just before.
Q. Do you have a copy of it?
A. Not in front of me, actually
Q. We can sort that out for you. Are you satisfied that
the content of the statement is, to the best of your
knowledge, true and correct?
A. Yes, I am. Thank you very much.
MR MUSTON: That document is tendered as exhibit L20,
Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, thanks. I've found mine as well.
MR MUSTON: Q. Could I ask you to go to paragraph 10 of
your statement, which is at the end of a passage where you
tell us about what you perceive to be some of the benefits
of rural placements during one's medical education?
A. Yes.
Q. You tell us that you had a very positive experience of
O&G in Griffith?
A. Yes, I did.

Q. You have told us in some little detail there but could
you just explain what it was about that rural placement
that you found to be a particularly positive experience?
A. I think the distinct difference between my rural
placement in Griffith, which is a relatively small
obstetrics department, and my other placement, which was in
the Royal Hospital for Women, which is probably the largest
obstetrics department in the state, was the amount of
individual focus and experience that I had.
When I was in the Royal Hospital for Women I was one
of I think four or five medical students. There was
a large number of interns and residents, there were senior
resident medical officers as well as registrars as well and
also fellows, so when it came to a division of
opportunities to learn, engage and perform procedures,
there were just simply divided by virtue of a large number
of people who were ahead of me, if you like, in the
training food chain; whereas when I was in Griffith it was
just myself and one other registrar, so I was able to get
much more hands on, I felt like my individual learning
needs and experiences were tailored.
I wasn't asked to leave or forgo learning
opportunities because there was not enough space in the
room or the patient or the woman had already seen X number
of people already who were there to teach as opposed to
deliver clinical care. So I felt overall I learnt a lot
more, was a bigger part of the team and it was a much more
enriching experience.
Q. You obviously have not chosen to pursue a career in
that area of specialisation?
A. Yes.
Q. What is it which has kept you working in the metro,
having had that good experience in a rural setting?
A. I suppose it was the duration of the experience, I was
there for four weeks. I had an enjoyable four weeks but it
was one of many rotations in medical school and after that
I would have done - I believe that was at the beginning of
year 6, I would have done another five or six placements in
different fields back in Sydney. And I did actually think
about doing obstetrics for a bit, but then I didn't get
a term, an internship and then it becomes hard to get
a term from then on and then you start pursuing other

things and, all of a sudden, unless you're really targeting
a particular specialty, it can be quite hard to later go
into it. So I suppose, you know, I became distracted and
other opportunities availed themselves is the reason
I didn't ultimately proceed to obstetrics.
Q. Based on experience you have of your cohort of junior
doctors, do you have a sense that those who have a longer
stretch of rural experience as part of their training
pathway are more likely to or, in your experience --
A. Yes.
Q. -- do stick in rural areas?
A. That's certainly the sense I get. For example,
I think I have put in my statement that of the two-thirds
of people who do a rural placement in their final year at
my medical school, I'd - sorry, of the people who did
a rural placement in their final year, I would estimate
two-thirds of them would stay to do a rural internship.
Anecdotally there's very few people I know of, maybe
like a handful, one or two as outliers, who would have done
their final years of medical school placement in the city
and then gone, "I'd like to go to a rural hospital
preferentially". When it comes to an internship, it's just
not an experience that I think people have.
Q. In terms of the sort of things that might persuade
people, junior doctors, to work in rural settings or to
move away from metro settings where some of those social
hooks might tend to draw them, do you have a view about
what the system might be able to do to encourage people to
move into different areas of the state to work?
A. I think you're right to say that people do get hooked
in and, to a certain extent, that's what keeps people
wanting to be in the same place. It doesn't just happen in
terms of the city or not, it even happens in terms of the
part of the city you are in.
People who tend to do their internship at Liverpool or
Westmead tend to gravitate towards registrar jobs in that
part of town. People who do their internship in Newcastle
tend to stay in Newcastle.
I think part of the way that you can assist people
with a bit of mobility is to, one, give them student
experience in that more rural location, so no longer do

they have hooks, say, in Sydney and they're less willing to
go.
Another thing you can do is make it easy to transition
between it. If I wanted to go rural now, it would honestly
be quite difficult. I have no connections to any rural
hospital from a personal perspective. I'd need to seek it
out myself and apply in my own time, maybe travelling at
significant expense, and there would be no guarantee I'd
have a job and I'd apply for it, and then I'd also have to
apply for all the others, and I would be fairly willing to
say that a place I know, which I already have connections
in, is going to give me a job preferentially and going to
give me advanced notice of that prior to me getting a job
in a rural location.
Q. Can I just unpack that a little bit?
A. Yes.
Q. We will come back to the process of applying that
you've touched on and you've referred to in your statement,
but what is it about the system that means if you happen to
be in a metro area or in particular metro hospital, the
ability for you to secure employment elsewhere is, at least
in your view, compromised?
A. I think people preferentially try and stay at their
hospital, regardless of where that hospital is, partially
for the familiarity, they know the systems, they know the
people; partially hospitals, to a certain extent, do try
and recruit people who have already been there, especially
in their junior years.
If people are going to a different hospital, it's
usually one that they have some kind of linkage too. For
example, one of the consultants that I worked with at RPA
also worked at St Vincent's so I informally inquired, "Do
you think there is likely to be a job there?" "Yes, there
is", and you fill in gaps, as such, that way as opposed to
a more national or statewide recruiting process.
It is easier to go somewhere that you know, that is
familiar, and it's harder if the place is somewhat
distanced, you don't have the connections, you don't have
the social support, you don't really know what you're
getting yourself into.
Q. I gather from some of the answers you have just given,

in part there is the candidate feels, "The better the devil
you know, I don't necessarily want to move to another
hospital or to a local health district that I'm not
familiar with if I can stay working where I am at the
moment." But also in part, is it your sense that those
same considerations inform who the hospitals choose to
employ into junior medical positions?
A. I think for most jobs in the hospitals, while
I haven't sat on the panel, I have a reasonably good sense
that there's a preferred set of candidates before the job's
advertised, and the most common circumstance is those
candidates do go on to obtain those jobs, pending something
extremely unforeseen happening in the process.
Q. Do you get the sense that that, perhaps driven even by
your own experience and the choices that you've made
professionally - does that drive people, as junior doctors
just embarking on their careers, into positions within the
metro hospitals?
A. I think yes in an answer - but to unpack that a little
bit further, the main reason I think people want to go to
metropolitan inner city teaching hospitals for internship
is because they're perceived to be the best for your
career. They'll give you the best training, they'll give
you the best experience, the best knowledge, the best
ability to go and get that next job.
So I think once that has occurred, then people - well,
they're already in these big hospitals, because that's
where the most majority of jobs are, but they desperately
want to stay there and the cycle perpetuates itself.
If you say - you know, the advice that you hear
commonly given is someone wants to do something, say, like
cardiothoracic surgery and, say, they're an international
graduate, they're not guaranteed an inner city teaching
hospital job, do one year at that hospital and then you can
apply and come more centrally for your resident year. And
anecdotally, resident jobs, it's quite easy to obtain and
then move into one of the more junior level jobs at a large
hospital and then people try their best to stay.
Q. Whether the perception be right or wrong, is there any
particular perception or view out there to the effect that
training or starting your career in that big metro hospital
is going to be better for you professionally in some way?
A. I think there is a perception there to a certain

extent and for certain specialties. For example, I would
say RPA has a very good reputation for basic physicians
training, so people want to try to get to RPA because they
have a major exam and they know that it's associated with
having a lot of support to get people through that exam.
Then, once you've got through that exam, you can focus on
other elements of your training.
That reputation doesn't exist to the same extent for
more rural hospitals. I think that's partially because
there's more work and there's not as much staff so there's
less of a focus or a perceived - perception that there will
be less of a focus on the individual professional
development.
Q. You tell us in paragraph 11 of your statement that you
believe there to be some scope within recruitment processes
to better link rural work to positions offered in those
perhaps more popular metropolitan positions. Could you
unpack that a little bit and explain what you had in mind?
A. Well, I would start by saying that I think most
people, especially if they're looking to get into a medical
specialty, would be willing to work essentially anywhere,
if they have the guarantee that they're going to go and
progress in that specialty.
I certainly, if I knew that I could have, you know,
gotten on the training scheme a bit earlier than I have,
that I'd have to do some rural time, I would have signed up
in a heartbeat ages ago.
The reason I make that point is I think if you were to
offer rural training and have that training accredited and
account for people progressing towards a career goal, I
think people would jump on it very, very quickly, as
opposed to doing unaccredited training or other jobs, even
if they're in more desirable or prestigious locations.
Q. So to the extent that it's within the power of the
system, if we could use that broadly, as a combination of
the colleges acting in consort, to locate training
positions in rural areas - that is to say, accredited
training positions in rural areas - it's your view that, at
least in areas which might be seen as desirable from
a training and career progression point of view - that is
to say, areas of practice - you could draw people into the
regions using that?

A. I think there would be very few junior medical
officers wanting to become specialty registrars who would
reject an accredited training position regardless of
location. I think there would be unique family
circumstances for some but I think the majority view is
"I'll take that opportunity, yes, please."
Q. You tell us in paragraph 12 that, at least as you
understand the current arrangements, some of the programs
involve relatively short stints in rural settings which -
do we gather from that that you think a short visit like
your four-week visit to a rural setting, as positive an
experience as it was, is not really going to drive people
into areas of need?
A. I think it enriches your training experience, but will
it determine that that person's future career prospects?
I don't think a short stint really will because I think you
keep your home base in Sydney, for example. You don't stop
paying rent, you go back every week end, you keep your
social connections. Where if it's a longer placement where
you're more ingrained in the community, you actually you
have to - you know, "I'm now from Dubbo", for example, as
opposed to, "I'm from Camperdown but I moved to Dubbo for
two months". I think it changes your mindset and how you
think with your future.
Q. Just from the perspective of a junior doctor, do you
have a view about the sort of time frame that we might be
looking at in order to become someone who is from Dubbo as
opposed to a --
A. I would be thinking 12 months, in that kind of sphere.
Q. Do you think that there might be some scope, just
coming back to the observation you make in paragraph 11,
for a greater connectivity to be built or a greater sense
of local connection to be built through an arrangement
whereby someone spends part of their time in the metro and
part in a rural setting, or do you think you really need to
have that consolidated period of full-time practice in a
rural setting, say your 12 months, in order to really start
to build that proper connection?
A. It's a good question. I'm honestly not sure if you
did, say, six months rural, six months city, six months
rural, six months city, that would give you - that would
have you feel more ingrained.
I don't know about that. What I do know is that the

current situation, for example, four weeks of medical
school, three months for a quarterly term rotation, is not
enough to do that. For example, my housemates have both
done rural placements, they both kept paying rent, they
both came up every other weekend and they were getting
through this period of rural placement and then they were
going to come back home to Sydney. It was never considered
that they may stay there. That didn't enter their mindset.
Q. And not necessarily inviting you to express an opinion
on what your housemates are or are not planning to do, but
it's your view if, instead of that arrangement, someone, as
part of their training, was required to spend, say,
12 months in a location like Dubbo or Wagga or somewhere
like that, that the chances of them becoming more closely
connected with that community and potentially seeing
a career path there would be enhanced?
A. I think that you become much more part of that
hospital system. It'd be not a place you're passing
through, it'd be a place that you are potentially settling
down in or developing roots, developing connections. When
it comes to apply for the job the next year, you already
know the people there, "Maybe this is where I might go", as
opposed to, "I'm not even thinking about it. I'm just
temporary, visiting."
Q. You tell us in paragraph 14 about the way in which the
recruitment campaign for the junior medical officers works?
A. Yes.
Q. You point to some opportunities for streamlining.
Could I ask you to just tell us a little bit about your own
experience in engaging with that process?
A. Yes, certainly. So you have a guaranteed job for your
first two years as an intern and a resident, then you need
to apply for apposition. Depending on what that position
is, you may need to apply every year. For surgery, as
I went into, that was my experience. I knew I wanted to do
neurosurgery. I knew I had no guarantee of getting a job
because it's relatively competitive, especially for people
who've just finished residency. So I applied for every
job, every neurosurgery job in New South Wales, of which
there were, I think, 18 to 20 or so.
Q. When you describe them as neurosurgery jobs, was that
a combination of accredited and unaccredited positions?
A. Only unaccredited jobs.

Q. So they were one-year contracts?
A. Yes.
Q. To work as a registrar within a neurosurgery
department, in a capacity that did not, other than building
your experience, contribute to your training, in a way that
was recognised?
A. That's correct. And I should add, those jobs also
were not guaranteed. So I also applied for senior resident
medical officer jobs in surgery and those jobs are also not
guaranteed. So I also applied for senior resident medical
officer jobs in general.
Q. How many --
A. About 30 applications.
Q. And in terms of the process, each was a separate
application?
A. Each was an individual separate application.
Q. And was it something that you could just copy and
paste and send the same words to each prospective or for
each prospective job, or not that simple?
A. There was a deal of similarity and the questions were
on the same vein but they were not the same. So for
example, one might be, "Please describe your experiences of
teamwork and how that is involved in patient care." And
the other one might be, "Please describe your experience of
teamwork and leadership." Just different enough that if
you copied the same thing into everything and someone was
looking at the questions, they would go, "This bloke is not
quite answering the question. He has applied for 30
different jobs he doesn't want to come here."
So, of course, you're individually tinkering to show
that you actually have read the question and that's quite
time-consuming. I don't think the answers were
substantially different, but they couldn't be copied and
pasted.
Q. And you did this each year up until --
A. Yes.
Q. -- the most recent occasion when you did it, which
secured your position as an accredited training position?
A. Yes, that's correct. So I have a little folder, if

you like, of all my previous applications and the questions
do change very slightly each year, so I'd go and very
slightly change the answers. So I became more efficient
with the process but it would still take me many hours each
year.
Q. As a ballpark, the first time you did it, how many
hours did it take?
A. I probably spent 30 hours on it, which sounds like
a lot, but, you know, you've got no - I don't think I'm an
outlier, to be honest. I think every - you are competing
against lots of people, there's very little that
differentiates you. You're not going to let something
little go through, you're going to try and develop
something that puts you through as a solid applicant. As
I've grown on, I started to think that perhaps these things
are not given the weight that you might expect they are
when you're first applying to the process, and you think
"Geez, that's a bit silly", in retrospect, but I don't
think anyone is willing to take anyone's word for it and
say, "No, no, just write something generic, you'll be
right."
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Do you get asked about why you
want to be a neurosurgeon?
A. No.
Q. You don't?
A. No, I didn't get asked that.
MR MUSTON: Q. You said a moment ago you're not an
outlier. It's your sense, discussing this process with
your peers, that they go through a similar process each
year applying for a junior medical officer position?
A. Yes is the answer. Some are them are more
streamlined. I know basic physician trainees, for example,
they only have one interview, is my understanding. It's
like there is a panel style process. Not quite the same
for all specialties, though. I think especially when
you're starting out, there is an extremely large amount of
time that goes into applying for jobs. I have a friend,
for example, wanting to do anaesthetics. I think he
applied for something like 50 jobs or something very large
like that, with no guarantee he's going to get any of them.
Q. And the assumption that you make is that 30 different
groups of people in 30 different facilities or units around

the state spend time reading your application, amongst, no
doubt, many others?
A. Yes. I've talked to some of the people who go through
and do this process and the feedback they say is a lot of
these candidates are very hard to differentiate. They've
all got statements that are very well written. They've all
got CVs that look very similar. They don't know any of
them and so it's down to finer points, this person
published two papers, this person published one paper.
Call up the referee and check, actually this person is not
nearly as good as what might be said on the paper, but I've
heard it takes a very substantial period of time to drill
down the list of candidates to a pool you can potentially
interview.
Q. You indicate in your statement that, in part, it's
your view that a lot of that time is wasted because there
are jobs that you, and no doubt others, are applying for
that you don't realistically think you are actually going
to have to take; is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. Could you just explain why that is?
A. So I think especially when you've been through the
process a few times, you have a reasonable sense of perhaps
your position in the pack. So to take last year, for
example, I'd been a neurosurgery registrar for four years,
I'd just missed out on selection for the training program.
I was pretty confident that I was going to get an
unaccredited job.
Q. That is to say, at your hospital?
A. At my hospital, and I have good relationships with
people there. While I was pretty confident, I had no
certainty of that, nothing written down on paper, and if
you only apply for one job and you don't get a job and all
the jobs are gone, then potentially you are left without
something to do for the next year and that is a big
problem, financially, career progression-wise. So you go
through and you put all your applications in, once again,
because you need to cover your bases.
Q. And you mentioned a moment ago the challenge in
differentiating between candidates based on what they've
written. I infer from the evidence you gave earlier that
one thing that can and perhaps often is used to
differentiate between candidates is the experience you've

had with that potentially small sample of them who happen
to work in your hospital?
A. That's certainly the anecdotal appearance. People who
have performed well on the job the year before are likely
to be invited back.
Q. And as a result of that, in your case, for example,
you applied for 30 jobs, one of which you were fairly
confident that you were going to get --
A. Mmm.
Q. -- and 29 of which resulted in a range of no doubt
very busy people - I say this entirely uncritically of you,
it's the system - a range of very busy people across the
state considering your application carefully and perhaps
hoping that they might be able to secure you as an
unaccredited registrar in their facility?
A. Yes, that's the case. And then I did get some offers
for some of those jobs later on down the line but, some
weeks, presumably when other candidates had taken other
jobs and vacancies had been created and the list has been
whittled down. By that time, almost everyone already has
a job, there are very few candidates who no longer have
one, so you say, "Thank you but no thank you."
Q. Again, anecdotally, do you have a sense that the way
that process rolls out is that positions in what might be
perceived to be desirable locations like the metro
hospitals get filled first, and then once you run out of
candidates and there are more jobs than candidates, the
ones that are left unfilled are those in what might be
perceived to be less desirable rural and remote locations?
A. I think that that is the case. I wouldn't necessarily
say it's only rural and remote locations that are less
desirable. I think a big part of the desirability of a job
is how supportive they're going to be for your training,
whether or not that's accredited or unaccredited.
For example, I know that there are some hospitals,
even though they're not - you might not consider them to be
in the nicest parts of Sydney, have the reputation for
having the best training or the best support for getting
people on to training programs or making good consultants
and having the opportunity to get a consultant job at the
other end. So those jobs can sometimes be highly
desirable. On the other end, some hospitals in very nice
locations in Sydney that you would perceive to be highly

desirable may not have the right culture or may have
the reputation of not having good training and so people
have prioritised them lower.
Q. Again whether it be right or wrong, is it the case
that amongst junior medical officers who are applying for
positions and going through this annual cycle, there is
a strong word-of-mouth sense of - well, there's lots of
discussion about what's desirable and what's not desirable
in terms of places to go?
A. Almost entirely word of mouth. This isn't written
down anywhere. You can't really have a look at a job
application as advertised by the hospital and say, "Oh,
that one is going to be good". They all say that they're
great and supportive, but there are reputations that are
communicated amongst individuals.
Q. Such that if I - and I'm not about to - were to ask
you, "What's a desirable location and what's an undesirable
location in a particular area", chances are the answer you
would give me would be the same as another doctor of your
experience --
A. Yes.
Q. -- if they were sitting there in your position?
A. Yes, I think so
Q. In terms of that process, there are a few ways that it
might potentially be streamlined. The first is some form
of centralisation such that, as a bare minimum, only one
application had to be lodged for all of the jobs. Do you
have a view about how that system, at least from the
perspective of a junior doctor applying, might be better,
more doctor-friendly?
A. I think that system exists to a certain extent for
some specialties. Plastic surgery, I believe, for example,
has one centralised interview and one centralised
application process. I see no reason why it couldn't be
done for the broad categories of jobs, senior resident
medical officers, unaccredited cardiology trainees,
unaccredited respiratory trainees, basic physician
trainees, I think it would save a large amount of
administrative time for both the candidates applying and
also, at the other end, make it much easier to sift through
the applications and determine which ones you would like.
Q. So in your case, it may have resulted in three

applications, one for a surgical position, one for a senior
resident medical officer position, and a third for the
other position that I can't now recall but you told us a
moment ago.
A. Yes, in my first year when I was applying for those
30 jobs, had we had a centralised system, I would have
applied for three broad categories; that's correct.
Q. So it's only once you get beyond those early years
where you start to have to - you're starting to make these
individual applications or --
A. No, no. If I were to detail the categories for you,
for example, one might be a specialty specific training,
neurosurgery position. One might be surgery in general,
which is a slightly more junior position, and the other one
might be a resident role. So I think regardless of your
stage of training, everyone's going to be going for one of
those broad sets of categories.
Q. Coming back to something you said a little bit
earlier, if within that specialty category you applied
centrally and perhaps were asked what your priorities were
in terms of where you would like to go based on your
personal circumstances and no doubt these unwritten
reputational factors, if you were offered a training
position in some location that was not metro Sydney but it
was an accredited position, you presumably would, based on
what you have told us, have gone?
A. Yes, I absolutely would have, and I'd go further to
say I would imagine that you could count on your hand the
number of people each year who would turn down an
accredited training position in view of its location.
Q. That's because, from a career progression point of
view, securing one of these accredited positions is
something which is of such value that the geographic
challenges that might be presented are --
A. Yes, very much so. It's so desirable and also once
you have that, you have so much more certainty over your
career. You don't have to apply for a job the next year.
You've just got that ability to control some destiny over
your life that you're just going to jump in it and take it,
even if it means that you might have to move in order to
have it.

a career progression that you can - or career pathway that

is more secure for you from the point of view of it is
a secure path toward a fellowship?

Q. And the second part of it is, if I've understood you
correctly, you no longer having to apply each year for jobs
because once on that career pathway, at least in your area
of specialisation, you're employed for, what, a period of
four years?
A. Five.
Q. Five years on the pathway, but that's --

a massive change in mindset from going, you know, "I don't
know where I'm going next year,, I'm pretty sure I'm
staying here but I've got no certainty of that", as, let's
say, "I've got a contract, I'm going to Liverpool next
year. I know where I'm going to be, I know at the end of
next year, I'll have a job with that sense of certainty.
I don't know where it is going to be but I have no doubt I
will be given one." So it's a massive weight off your
shoulders that junior doctors don't really have in an
earlier stage.
Q. Can I ask you, you've told us a little bit in
paragraphs 16 to 18 about the potential benefits, at least
to the system, of unaccredited training roles?
A. Mmm.
Q. And as I understand what you tell us there, there are
benefits to the system of unaccredited registrars being
employed because there are aspects of the work that is
required to be done in departments, in surgical
departments, for example, which require a workforce --
A. Mmm.
Q. -- but there is insufficient procedures being done to
enable that workforce, every member of that workforce to be
accruing the training and experience they need as part of
their training pathway.
A. Mmm.
Q. From the perspective, though, of a junior doctor, do
you see any way in which that system might be reconfigured
so as to increase the number of accredited positions and
avoid the situation where you're having to go through this
process annually?

A. I understand the tension there. I think the challenge
is that for a lot of these specialties, neurosurgery,
cardiology, respiratory medicine, we only need so many
consultants at the other end. We don't necessarily need
more neurosurgeons in Australia. We have a lot more people
who want to go on and join these specialty workforces than
we actually have a need for. We do, however, need people
in the hospitals to do the grunt work, the background
service work, the on-call work, seeing the consults.
I don't have a good solution about how we could
necessarily increase the number of accredited training
positions and I believe the college of surgeons at least
accredits every spot that they're able to in terms of
volume. I do, however, think there is a problem for people
who are in an unaccredited situation and have no guarantee
or certainty for their future, because at the moment,
there's really two ways out. One is that you get on to the
training program and you finish, and that's fantastic, and
the other one, that the majority in some cases end up going
through, is that you leave, and all of your specialty
knowledge, all of your experience, all of your skill that
you've gotten up to that point essentially goes nowhere.
Maybe you use a little bit of it in a different role but
you're certainly not using it in the same capacity.
Q. So when you say you leave, what is it that they leave
to do? They cease to be an unaccredited registrar in
surgery having tried but failed to get on to an accredited
pathway?
A. Mmm.
Q. They then pursue a different specialisation or what is
it that they do?

radiology, a different kind of surgery, general practice.
Some people leave entirely, might do something - have
a career change, for example. I think it's wasteful of so
many years' specialty training, because these people are
probably very good doctors in the majority of cases, maybe
just not quite competitive enough because there are so few
spots available each year.
The solution I propose to this problem is to formalise
this unaccredited registrar role in a, say, career medical
officer style position. So, for example, you're no longer
every year applying to get on to the training program but

you've got a set number of hours, you've got a set contract
for probably longer than a year, you've got some certainty
about your career, and in a way, the pressure is off and
you know what you're going to be doing and you're able to
deliver your sub-specialty knowledge under the supervision
of a consultant as opposed to being stuck in the
unaccredited rat race trying each year and maybe not quite
getting there and maybe you're never going to quite get
there. I think that's the limbo that gets people really
stuck.

excess of junior workforce into the locum market.
A. Mmm.

unaccredited trainee could potentially be adjusted or used
to shift the balance in terms of that move into the locum
market - that is to say, do you see value in there being
a reward for loyal service to the system that doesn't
involve you going locuming?

really a reward that I can identify for being loyal to the
system. I'm going to apologise and say I don't have
a great solution here but I can elucidate the problem

For example, I had a conversation with someone only
a few weeks ago who was saying, "You know, I've got my
contract for next year, I think I'll just quit and locum
the rest of the year." "Why would you do that?" "The pay

overworked at the moment and I've got my ticket for next
year. Why would I stay?"

fellow staff, that person is probably going to burn their
bridges if they do do that at that hospital, but from their
perspective, you know, the quote would be, "The system
hasn't looked after me, why would I give back?"

was hoping for an accredited position in the facility or

that that decision to cut their contract and come back next

impact on their career progress?
A. I would go even further because the majority of these
specialty positions are actually centrally allocated and so
even if they do later get sent back to that facility, in a
way, it doesn't matter. They've got their training spot,
they get through that year, that hospital remembers them
poorly because of what they did, that's going to be awkward

with it. It's not going to have any long-term impact on

from letting down your colleagues.

things that advance people's individual career; less
desirable terms might be things like nights or relief duty.

contract, they've got one term left and it's nights, the
incentive to get up and go is pretty high; whereas if you
are doing nights as your last term but you know you're
going to have a great next few terms, people might be
incentivised to stick through that.

contract for a term of service, the year does not count in
terms of their eligibility to apply, in terms of points
they might get for career completion and things like that.

calculating the overall value of someone's CV. For

adjust - and I should mention, that overall ranking is then
used to compare different candidates. If you were to say

majorly change behaviour, because I think there would be
very few people who would be willing to quit right at the
end knowing that they are not going to get the value for
that year done.

specialty, it would need to be a tailored solution, but
certainly if you told people that unless they do the time,
the year is not going to count, that would change behaviour

used to differentiate people.
